name: Benin City
info: Benin City is the capital of Edo State in southern Nigeria and the historic seat of the Ọba of Benin, a city that grew rich on trade with Europeans, was burnt by a British force in 1897 and remains the home of an old monarchy.

facts.founded: According to tradition the land was first ruled by the Ogiso kings, and the present line of Ọba began when Prince Ọranmiyan of Ife sent his son to rule; Benin imperialism began in the last decade of the 13th century under Ọba Ewedo.
facts.where: In southern Nigeria, the capital of Edo State, within the local government areas of Egor, Ikpoba-Okha and Oredo.
facts.known: The Ọba and the kingdom of Benin; trade in pepper and ivory with the Portuguese; the city wall and moat; bronze casting and the Benin Bronzes; the British expedition of 1897
facts.today: Benin City is the capital and largest city of Edo State and the fourth-largest city in Nigeria by the 2006 census.

t: Benin City was the seat of the Ọba, whose line began, according to tradition, when a son of Ọranmiyan of Ife was set on the throne, and it grew rich in the 16th and 17th centuries on trade with Europeans in pepper and ivory.
On 17 February 1897 a British force of 1,200 men captured, sacked and burnt the city and took the bronzes from the palace, an act that opened the way to British colonisation.
The British allowed the monarchy to be restored in 1914, and after Nigeria's independence the city became the capital of the Mid-Western Region, of Bendel State and, from 1991, of Edo State.
dyk: In 1691 a Portuguese captain wrote that Great Benin was larger than Lisbon and that the people had no doors to their houses; in 1701 or 1702 a Dutch merchant called the same city a "mere village".

sections.origins:
Benin City stands in southern Nigeria, in a climate that is hot and humid through the year. Its indigenous people are the Edo, also called the Bini, who speak the Edo language. The city's early history is known chiefly through tradition. According to tradition, the first rulers of the Edo were the Ogiso, the "kings of the sky", who called the land Igodomigodo. Igodo was the first Ogiso and was succeeded by his eldest son Ere. A struggle for power followed between the wife of the last Ogiso and his son, Prince Ekaladerhan, who was framed by her and sentenced to death. The men sent to kill him released him at Ughoton, and he went into exile and took a new name.

When the elders, led by Chief Oliha, searched for the banished prince, he refused to return and sent his son Ọranmiyan in his place. Ọranmiyan took up residence in a palace built for him at Uzama, now a coronation shrine. He married Ẹrinmwide, daughter of the ninth Enogie of Egor, and they had a son. Ọranmiyan renounced his office, calling the land Ile-Ibinu, a land of vexation, and had his son made king. Ọba Ẹwẹka later renamed the capital Ubinu, a name the Portuguese reinterpreted as Benin. Yoruba tradition tells the story differently, but both the Yoruba and the Edo agree that Oduduwa sent Ọranmiyan of Ife to rule Benin City and that he founded the Ọba dynasty there.
sections.growth:
Benin imperialism began in the last decade of the 13th century under Ọba Ewedo. Around 1470 Ẹwuare changed the name of the state to Ẹdo, about the time the people of Ọkpẹkpẹ migrated from the city. The Portuguese visited Benin City around 1485, and the city grew rich during the 16th and 17th centuries through trade within southern Nigeria and with Europeans, mostly in pepper and ivory. In the early 16th century the Ọba sent an ambassador to Lisbon, and the King of Portugal sent Christian missionaries to Benin.

European visitors compared the city to their own. A Portuguese captain, Lourenco Pinto, described it in 1691: "Great Benin, where the king resides, is larger than Lisbon; all the streets run straight and as far as the eye can see." He wrote that the king's house was large and richly decorated, with fine columns, that the city was wealthy and industrious, and that it was so well governed that theft was unknown and the people had no doors to their houses. The people of the region also farmed yam, plantain and cassava for subsistence. A large rampart and ditch, the Benin city wall or moat, surrounded the city, and the inhabited town of the 19th century lay about a mile beyond it.
sections.rulers:
According to tradition the Ogiso dynasty ruled the land first, and the Ọba line began when Ọranmiyan's son became king. In one account Ọranmiyan's son Ajaka ultimately became the first Ọba of Benin of the present line, while Ọranmiyan himself reigned as Ọọni of Ifẹ. Ẹwẹka I was an Ọba of Benin, and Ewedo began the expansion of the state in the last decade of the 13th century. Ẹwuare changed the state's name to Ẹdo around 1470.

On 17 February 1897 the city fell to the British. The expedition's force of 1,200 men was under Admiral Sir Harry Rawson. The capture of Benin opened the way to British colonisation, and the kingdom was merged into the Niger Coast Protectorate, then the Protectorate of Southern Nigeria and finally the Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria. The British permitted the restoration of the Benin monarchy in 1914, but true political power still lay with the colonial administration of Nigeria.

After Nigeria's independence in 1960, Benin City became the capital of the Mid-Western Region when that region was split from Western Region in June 1963. In 1976 the region was renamed Bendel State, and the city remained its capital. It became the capital of Edo State in 1991, when Bendel State was divided into Delta State and Edo State.
sections.life:
The Edo are the indigenous people of Benin City. They have one of the richest dress cultures on the African continent and are known for their beads, which stand for royalty and stand out at traditional marriages, as well as for body marks, bangles, anklets and raffia work. The Bini have four market days: Ekioba, Ekenaka, Agbado and Eken.

The Binis are known for bronze sculpture and casting. Igun Street in the city is known for bronze casting and other metal work. The Benin Bronzes were portrait figures, busts and groups made in iron, carved ivory and especially in brass, which is conventionally called bronze. Contact with the Portuguese left its mark on language: some residents of Benin could still speak a pidgin Portuguese in the late 19th century, and many Portuguese loan words are still found in the languages of the area.

The Igue festival is held each year to usher in the new year and is believed to renew Ọba Ewuare's magical powers; it comes between the Christmas and New Year celebrations and includes the Ọba's blessing of the land and his people. Human sacrifice was reported in the city by Alan Boisragon, a survivor of the Benin Massacre, in an account of 1898. The historian James D. Graham notes that there is little doubt that sacrifice was an integral part of the Benin state religion from very early days, but that first-hand accounts varied significantly, some reporting it and others making no mention of it.
sections.crises:
By the 18th and 19th centuries visitors found the city smaller than before. In a letter of 1701 or 1702 the Dutch East India Company merchant David van Nyendael described Benin City as a "mere village". He praised the king's palace, with its turreted roofs decorated with brass snakes, and called the intact houses "large and handsome", but noted that the town had clearly been more densely populated in the past and was now mostly "half-ruined houses". In 1820 a British naval officer, Lieutenant John King, wrote that the walls had been largely destroyed and that the city had formerly been depopulated by a civil war, so that its inhabited area did not exceed two or three miles in circumference.

In 1897 a British delegation led by Acting Consul General James Robert Phillips was ambushed, and all but two of its men were killed. The British answered with what they called a Punitive Expedition. A force of 1,200 men under Admiral Sir Harry Rawson captured Benin City on 17 February 1897, sacked it and burnt it. Reginald Bacon, a member of the expedition, described the town that he found as an irregular straggling town of groups of houses separated by patches of bush, about a mile and a half from east to west and a mile from north to south. The force looted the palace. Some of the bronzes were auctioned to cover the expenses of the capture and occupation of the city.
sections.legacy:
The Benin Bronzes were looted from the palace by the expeditionary force. Most of them are today in western museums at locations around the world, and in recent years appeals have gone to various museums and governments to return them. The best-known of them, the Queen Idia mask, was used as the mascot of the Second Festival of Arts and Culture (FESTAC '77), held in Nigeria in 1977, and is now known as the Festac Mask.

Benin City is the home of one of the oldest ongoing monarchies in the world. The Oba's palace, the National Museum, the Benin moats, King's Square and the city's traditional markets mark the old city. The Benin moats measure about 20 to 40 feet.

Benin City is today the capital and largest city of Edo State in southern Nigeria. By the 2006 census it was the fourth-largest city in Nigeria, after Lagos, Kano and Ibadan. It is one of the principal commercial and industrial centres in the south of the country and the centre of Nigeria's rubber industry, and palm oil and palm kernels are significant exports. The University of Benin is among its institutions of higher learning.

summary: Benin City, in southern Nigeria, was the seat of the Ọba of Benin and grew rich on trade in pepper and ivory with the Portuguese. A British force burnt it and took its bronzes in 1897. It is now the capital of Edo State.
notes: START: the article gives no founding date for the city. I used c. 1290 (circa true), the one date it gives for the Edo state acting as an empire (Ewedo's imperialism, 'last decade of the thirteen century'). Editor may prefer another start.
The source is short (about 2,500 words) and has no history-of article. Sections are written only from it; some run under or near the guide's lengths rather than be padded.

Tradition is internally inconsistent in the article: Ọranmiyan is said to leave a son who becomes king, and 'his son Ajaka ultimately became the first Oba of Benin of the present line' while also 'the father of Ẹwẹka I'; the article also says Ọranmiyan was Ọọni of Ifẹ and Ajaka Alaafin of Ọyọ. I kept only Ajaka as in the article and Ẹwẹka I as an Ọba, and did not reconcile them. The article's passage about Ekaladerhan 'whom the Ife now called Oduduwa' is garbled; I wrote 'took a new name' and 'Oduduwa sent Ọranmiyan' only where the final sentence states it.
'Around 1470 Ẹwuare changed the name of the state to Ẹdo': the article spells the Ọba as Ẹwuare and Ewuare (Igue festival). Ọba Ewedo's name is as given.

Lourenco Pinto's description is dated 1691 in the article, although the article introduces it with 16th and 17th century accounts; kept as given. Whether the 1701 'mere village' and the 1691 account refer to the same condition is not for the text to settle.

Admiral Rawson's force: the article says 'a 1,200-strong British force'. The phrase 'Punitive Expedition' is the article's own quotation marks. Casualties and the number of Benin dead are not given; no figures were added.

Looting: the article says the bronzes were 'looted from the Benin City palace by the expeditionary force' and that some were auctioned to cover the expedition's costs. It gives no count of objects and no list of museums; I gave none.
Human sacrifice is given as Graham and Boisragon give it, with the article's note that accounts varied. I did not state how often or on what scale.

The article says the walls 'had been to a large extent destroyed' and the inhabited area 'does not now exceed two or three miles' (King, 1820); I wrote 'two or three miles in circumference' as the article gives it. The 'town located about a mile beyond the large surrounding rampart' is as stated.
Moat measure ('about 20 to 40 ft') is given in feet in the article and kept.

Left out: climate details, flooding and waste management, schools and universities beyond one mention, airport, festivals other than Igue, notable people, the Benin City Film Festival. The 'Vadoo day' and festival list are unclear and left out. Population figures: the article gives none, only the 2006 census rank.
Archaeological and city-wall dating are not in the article; the origins section therefore rests on tradition alone and does not give archaeology.
